title: Hyperclique Hypothesis
formal: Is the following bounded-error randomized Hyperclique Hypothesis true? For every fixed pair of integers \(h\ge3\) and \(k>h\), and every constant real \(\epsilon>0\), there is no uniform classical randomized word-RAM algorithm \(A\) and constant \(T\ge1\) such that for every \(n\ge k\) and every simple \(h\)-uniform hypergraph \(H\) on \([n]\), \(A\) outputs one bit deciding whether \(H\) contains a \(k\)-clique, runs for at most \(Tn^{k-\epsilon}\) steps on every execution, and is correct with probability at least \(2/3\) on that input. The dense representation, permitted instructions and word size are fixed below. The program and constants may depend on \(h,k,\epsilon\), but not on \(n\), the input hypergraph or the random outcomes.
definitions:
Write \([n]=\{1,\ldots,n\}\) and \(\binom{[n]}h=\{e\subseteq[n]:|e|=h\}\). The hypergraph is \(H=([n],E)\) for an arbitrary set \(E\subseteq\binom{[n]}h\): hyperedges are unordered sets of distinct vertices, with no weights, repetitions, colors or other promises. A \(k\)-clique is a subset \(S\subseteq[n]\) of cardinality \(k\) satisfying \(\binom Sh\subseteq E\). Only existence is queried; a witness, count or list is not required. Inputs with \(n<k\) have answer zero and may be handled separately. Uniformity \(h\) and clique size \(k\) are fixed constants for each algorithm under consideration, not growing input parameters.

The input stores \(n\) and a dense read-only membership array with one word for each increasing tuple \(1\le v_1<\cdots<v_h\le n\), ordered lexicographically. That word is exactly \(1\) if \(\{v_1,\ldots,v_h\}\in E\), and \(0\) otherwise, with all unused bits zero. There is no auxiliary input index or precomputed data structure. The RAM may access this array at a computed address; each probe is charged. All preprocessing, auxiliary table construction, arithmetic and output are charged. The algorithm is not required to scan the entire array if it can obtain the answer with fewer probes.

For a fixed algorithm choose an integer \(D\ge h+1\) and let the word length be \(w=D\lceil\log_2(n+2)\rceil\) bits. The constant \(D\) can depend on the fixed \(h,k,\epsilon\), but not on \(n\) or \(E\). Registers, addresses and memory cells contain unsigned \(w\)-bit words; initially work memory is zero. In one step the machine may read or write a word at a word-sized address, copy a word, compare words, branch, use a bitwise Boolean operation, shift, add, subtract or multiply modulo \(2^w\), or take unsigned integer quotient or remainder with nonzero divisor. A shift by at least \(w\) yields zero. Each random instruction produces a fresh independent uniform \(w\)-bit word in one step. Computations involving larger integers require charged multiword operations. There is no unit-cost real or arbitrary-precision arithmetic, oracle or quantum operation, and no advice depending on \(n\). The program has one finite description for all sizes; input-independent constants in that fixed description are allowed, but generated tables cost time.

Success probability is over these random words for each fixed hypergraph. It may have two-sided error, but must be at least \(2/3\) on every positive and every negative input. The time bound holds on all random executions, including erroneous ones; expected time alone is a different guarantee. No separate space bound is imposed beyond the addressed-word model and charged computation. The exclusion concerns every fixed pair \((h,k)\) separately and every fixed positive exponent saving, not only a limit as \(k\) grows. Writing the time bound for all \(n\ge k\) is equivalent to the asymptotic big-O convention: finitely many exceptional sizes can be handled by a finite modification of the algorithm and its constant. One may restrict to rational positive savings without changing the hypothesis, since any positive saving implies a smaller rational saving.
answer_criterion: Give a complete mathematically correct proof checked in Lean of the entire stated exclusion, or a complete Lean-checked refutation. A proof of the hypothesis must cover every fixed \(h\ge3,k>h\), every positive saving and every randomized algorithm in the specified model; a conditional lower bound alone is insufficient. A refutation supplies one fixed pair \((h,k)\), one \(\epsilon>0\), a finite algorithm and constants, and proves its worst-case bound and per-input success probability for all hypergraphs of every size. It need not improve all parameter pairs and need not print a clique. Saving only a logarithmic factor, using expected time without the required worst-case guarantee, exploiting a proper promised subclass, or proving a restricted or nonuniform algebraic circuit bound does not settle this statement. This is an exact yes/no hypothesis about asymptotic resources, with no additive numerical tolerance.
why: A principal fine-grained hypothesis for higher-order combinatorial interactions, supporting conditional lower bounds beyond ordinary graph clique and shortest paths.

importance.reason: A foundational unresolved exponent question with consequences for Max-CSP optimization, algebraic identity checking and sparse graph/hypergraph algorithms.

progress.text: Lincoln–Vassilevska Williams–Williams develop hyperclique hypotheses, their Max-h-SAT connections and conditional graph-algorithm lower bounds.
Fischer–Künnemann–Redžić–Stieß prove regularization preserving fine-grained clique complexity and apply it to Boolean CSP optimization.
Dudek and coauthors relate the 3-uniform 4-hyperclique hypothesis to arithmetic-progression detection in their STOC 2026 study of algebraic identities.
Fritsch–Künnemann–Redžić–Stieß analyze when sparsity helps for hypergraph independent sets and use hyperclique assumptions for matching lower bounds.
A tensor-complexity report states and uses an explicitly nonuniform algebraic hyperclique assumption; it does not prove the classical algorithmic hypothesis.
The revised partition-rank paper gives general connections to algebraic circuit lower bounds while leaving its hyperclique application conjectural.

status_note: Checked through 16 September 2026. No classical bounded-error word-RAM algorithm with a fixed positive exponent saving on all inputs for a covered pair, or unconditional proof of the full exclusion, was found in the bounded primary-source review. The 2025 regularization and 2026 arithmetic-progression and sparsity papers state conditional consequences. The February 2026 nonuniform algebraic variant and August partition-rank result do not prove this randomized algorithmic hypothesis. External proofs were not independently certified.

context_blocks.text: A graph records pairwise compatibility; an \(h\)-uniform hypergraph records compatibility of \(h\) vertices at a time. For \(h=3\) and \(k=4\), a positive instance has four vertices whose four triples are all hyperedges. Having each pair participate in some hyperedge elsewhere does not establish these four triples on the same vertex set. This is the smallest parameter pair covered by the hypothesis.

For fixed \(h,k\), direct inspection of all \(k\)-vertex sets gives \(O(n^k)\) time, since each set has only \(\binom{k}{h}\) hyperedges to check. The task is therefore polynomial-time for every fixed parameter pair. The hypothesis concerns a constant reduction in that polynomial exponent; NP-hardness with a variable clique-size parameter is a different assertion.

The graph case \(h=2\) behaves differently. Matrix multiplication gives algorithms beating the direct k-tuple search for many clique sizes. Lincoln–Vassilevska Williams–Williams explain why the corresponding higher-order operation for hypergraphs is a separate obstacle and formulate hyperclique-based lower bounds. This distinction is the reason the present hypothesis starts at \(h=3\), instead of extending a graph-clique bound mechanically to all uniformities.

Their connections to satisfiability concern optimization problems such as Max-h-SAT: find an assignment satisfying as many clauses as possible. A suitable hyperclique speedup would also improve exhaustive-search algorithms for these problems. This must be distinguished from deciding whether every clause of a fixed-width SAT instance is simultaneously satisfiable, for which exponential improvements are already known. The Max-h-SAT hypothesis is an additional assumption, not an unconditional proof.

The fixed exponent saving is essential. A running time \(n^{k}\) divided by any fixed power of log n would not contradict the card. Nor would an improvement available only when k grows with n. Conversely, an \(O(n^{3.99})\) algorithm for 4-cliques in 3-uniform hypergraphs would be enough to refute the universally quantified statement, without resolving every other h,k pair.

The dense encoding has \(\binom nh=\Theta(n^h)\) Boolean entries for fixed \(h\). Since \(k>h\), conversions taking \(n^h\) times logarithmic factors do not erase every positive exponent saving: a claimed saving can always be weakened to a smaller positive constant. There is no promise that the input has few hyperedges, few nonedges or a particular distribution.

The inherited hypothesis is stated for \(k\)-partite hypergraphs. In that setting vertices are divided into \(k\) parts and each hyperedge uses distinct parts; a clique has one vertex in each part. For fixed \(h,k\), standard conversions between general and partite instances have a constant-factor vertex increase and preserve a positive exponent saving after charging their input-processing time. The card states the equivalent general-input detection task.

Fischer, Künnemann, Redžić and Stieß prove a stronger regularization theorem. For each fixed \(h<k\), their Theorem 3.1 converts an arbitrary hypergraph to a \(k\)-partite one with only a parameter-dependent constant-factor vertex increase, preserving whether a \(k\)-clique exists. The output has equal extension counts for transversal subsets of each size below \(h\). Thus this strong regularity promise does not by itself remove the conditional fine-grained difficulty.

The same work uses regularization to classify optimization of Boolean CSPs over assignments with exactly k nonzero variables. The degree of the constraint functions separates easy linear cases, graph-clique cases and higher-degree cases with exhaustive-search lower bounds under a 3-uniform hyperclique assumption. This supplies a reason to study the hypothesis beyond the clique problem itself.

Dudek and coauthors’ STOC 2026 work relates \((k-1)\)-uniform \(k\)-hypercliques to detecting \(k\)-term arithmetic progressions in a bounded integer universe. For the smallest case and a fixed \(0<\epsilon<1\), an \(O(n^{4-\epsilon})\)-time hyperclique algorithm would give an \(O(N^{2-\epsilon/2})\)-time algorithm for four-term progression detection in \(X\subseteq\{0,\ldots,N\}\), by Lemma 5.7. Here \(N\) is the universe bound, not merely \(|X|\). This is a conditional connection; neither side is proved hard unconditionally.

Fritsch–Künnemann–Redžić–Stieß’s ICALP 2026 paper studies when sparsity helps for small independent sets in hypergraphs and Boolean CSPs. Its algorithms have separate vertex-count and edge-count terms, with matching bounds under clique hypotheses. Improved running time on sparse forbidden-hyperedge inputs is compatible with the dense worst-case statement here; taking a complement can turn a sparse instance into a dense one.

The February 2026 report Beyond Bilinear Complexity states a separate nonuniform algebraic hyperclique conjecture about circuit families computing a hyperclique tensor. Its Theorem 4 derives a failure of circuit-complexity submultiplicativity from that assumption. The authors explicitly distinguish this circuit hypothesis from a uniform algorithmic consequence. It is not a proof of the randomized word-RAM lower bound on this card.

Brand, Kaski and Wang’s August 2026 revision relates partition ranks to multiplicative complexity of multilinear maps. Its hyperclique discussion concerns potential algebraic circuit lower bounds; it does not establish the required exponent bound even for the hyperclique polynomial, nor does it give an exponent-saving classical detection algorithm. The computational models and the conjectural status remain separate.

The hypothesis expresses a possible computational divide between pairwise and higher-order interactions. Its value is that precise reductions turn it into concrete runtime barriers for other tasks. The proper status is a conjectural foundation for those barriers. Repeated applications and increasingly robust reductions strengthen its usefulness, while a proof or one genuine exponent-saving algorithm would be a qualitatively different result.

sentences: A k-clique in an h-uniform hypergraph is a set of k distinct vertices containing every possible h-element hyperedge.
The hypothesis excludes a fixed positive improvement over the exhaustive-search exponent for every fixed uniformity at least three and every larger fixed clique size.
The chosen model is a uniform classical randomized word-RAM on a dense membership table, with worst-case time and success probability at least two thirds for each input.
A complete Lean proof must establish the full exclusion or give one fixed parameter pair and a proved exponent-saving algorithm that refutes it.
Conditional reductions, sparse-input improvements and nonuniform algebraic circuit results from the 2026 literature do not settle this all-input randomized hypothesis.
